A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Quest, with matching core algorithms and experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original continued-pretraining evaluations, retrieval experiments, scaling-law fits, and ablations, including Tables 1–3 and Sections 5–6.

after.justification: v6 retains original experiments and adds HELMET evaluations, keyword-quality assessments, and component analyses in Tables 12–17.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains query prediction, RAKE keyword extraction, inverted indexing, index splitting, and oversampled document concatenation. The added oversampling equations elaborate the existing procedure; the PDFs do not establish an algorithm change. Alternative keyword and document-selection strategies are evaluated as comparisons.

E1.justification: v6 adds HELMET's 17 subtasks, including retrieval-augmented generation and re-ranking, and a keyword-quality assessment task. Numeric-string retrieval extends from v3's 500k context scenario to 1M tokens. Pile training, LongBench, Longbook QA, and the seven short-text benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Qwen2.5-7B, and LLaMA-3.1-8B-base, while removing LLaMA-2-13B-64K. Figure 4 adds those three models and Yi-9B-200K to the needle comparison. Tables 14–17 introduce alternative keyword sources, highest-RAKE selection, and KNN selection variants. Standard, KNN, and ICLM remain the core synthesis baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include HELMET averaging across 8k, 16k, 32k, 64k, and 128k; controlled query-keyword corruption; and keyword-selection comparisons. Appendix C.3 introduces a five-point rating rubric, 100 samples assessed by two PhD students and GPT-4o, followed by 1,000 GPT-4o-rated samples. Existing Pythia training settings in Table 6 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendices C.2–C.4 and D.1 add analyses of query-keyword corruption, keyword extraction from queries versus documents or summaries, random versus highest-RAKE selection, and alternative KNN similarity rankings. These directly probe important design choices. Earlier training-progress, long-document, and split-ratio analyses remain; the split-ratio analysis moves to Appendix A.4.

E5.justification: Appendix C.3 adds correlation-based validation of automatic ratings, reporting Pearson correlation 0.7986 between human and GPT-4o scores on the 100-sample assessment. Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests for model performance.

E6.justification: Core Tables 1–3 and 5, detailed LongBench results, and scaling-law results are retained. New results include HELMET averages of 50.97 for Quest versus 48.08 for Standard, keyword-quality and selection outcomes, and additional baseline scores. Numeric retrieval is reported at 100% through 1M tokens instead of the earlier 500k evaluation; 128k sentence retrieval remains 97%, so this is expanded evidence rather than a same-setting accuracy gain.

T1.justification: Section 3 adds explicit mathematical definitions of oversampling sample allocation in Equations 1–2, introducing group sizes, an oversampling probability, and integer rounding. v3 described this allocation verbally. The scaling-law equation and algorithmic mathematics otherwise remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract expands the advertised context capability from 128k to 1M tokens, and Figure 1 claims the first base model achieving 100% accuracy at 1M on the specified retrieval task. The introduction also adds detailed analysis of Quest's design choices as an explicit contribution. The central synthesis and scaling-law claims remain.

C2.justification: v6 adds interpretations connecting query quality and random keyword selection to performance, attributes weaker summary-derived keywords to summaries' broader semantic space, and argues that matching document similarity alone cannot explain Quest's advantage. It also distinguishes sentence and numeric retrieval difficulty. v3's explicit warning about doc2query/RAKE biases disappears, although the computational limitation of larger query generators remains in Appendix C.2.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 newly reports synthesis costs: 24 hours on 16 H800 GPUs for query generation, then 0.5 and 3 hours on 128 CPUs for keywords and indexing. v6 clarifies equal-data controls and GPT-4-based retrieval scoring. Table 6's training configuration is retained, while the earlier disclosure of 32,768 KNN inverted lists is removed.

R1.justification: v6 adds references supporting newer comparisons and evaluations, including HELMET, LongVA, LWM, LLaMA 3.1/3.2, DeepSeek-V2, and Qwen2.5. It removes v3's explicit statement that earlier synthesis work was limited to 8k and adds the first-base-model-at-1M positioning. The related-work organization and central relationship to retrieval-based synthesis remain substantially intact.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around semantic relevance and diversity. Evaluation discussion is reorganized, analysis precedes scaling laws, split-ratio discussion moves into the appendix, and the standalone limitations section disappears. The appendices are reorganized around implementation, retained results, and new component analyses.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, with extensive figure and table relocation and revised captions. Figure 4 expands from two to six retrieval heatmaps, a 1M heatmap becomes Figure 1, and Tables 12–17 are added. The domain-distribution pies move to the appendix, while the earlier absolute-volume bar chart is removed.

improvement.justification: Tables 13–17 substantially address v3's limited direct evidence for query generation, keyword selection, and the advantage over similarity-based aggregation. HELMET broadens validation, and synthesis-cost reporting improves practical transparency. These gains outweigh the removed bias caveat and some overstatements, including Section 4.3's claim that Standard is worst at 128k, contradicted by Table 2 at 6.9B and 12B. The improvement rests primarily on stronger experimental support, not the larger context-length claim; run-to-run uncertainty remains unreported.
